summary: NHTSA retained the 50-pound weight reduction scenario applicable to GM, noting that GM did not claim weight reduction was impossible, and confirmed that the full weight-reduction impact would be attributed to GM's fleet in the agency's analysis.
text:
The manufacturers' comments on the impossibility of weight reduction are not incorporated because the application of weight reduction is only to GM and they did not say it was impossible. The discussion of sulfate emissions has been dropped and the discussion of noble metal use has been revised to indicate a smaller increase in the use of platinum and palladium. Minor changes have been made to the sections on noise emissions and increased use of plastics.
•
The most significant changes to the draft EIS are the inclusion of the possible effects on fuel economy of the MY 1979 emission standard and the provision for two classes of NPA's. These changes result from comments made by the domestic manufacturers on both the NPRM and the draft EIS. The agency is uncertain as to the final resolution of comments which produced these two changes. This is the reason for using a range of possible final AFES's.
Besides the changes in the emission standard for MY 1979, there are changes to the test procedures by which fuel economy is measured. These changes have

the effect of an apparent reduction in fuel economy when compared to the procedures in effect for MY 1976 from which fuel economy in MY 1979 was projected. The industry comments indicated a range of 6.2 percent to 10 percent for this apparent reduction in fuel economy. Gasoline savings from MY 1976 to MY 1979 must be determined relative to the same test procedures. Because of the uncertainty of the impact of the MY 1979 procedures, savings have been determined relative to the MY 1976 procedures. This means that the range of fuel economies for which gasoline savings are determined is based only on the possible fuel economy penalty of the MY 1979 emission standard. For the two possible classes of NPA's, the ranges of 14.9 mpg to 17.4 mpg for recreational-type NPA's with off-road capabilites reduces to 16.2 mpg to 17.4 mpg when the effect of the test procedure changes are deleted, the range of 16.4 mpg to 18.7 mpg for all other NPA's reduces to 17.8 mpg to 18.7 mpg.

Manufacturers of NPA's are planning substantial improvements in fuel economy by MY 1979. Because of these voluntary plans, the agency is uncertain how to estimate the impact of an average fuel economy standard applicable in MY 1979. On the one hand, it can be argued that all

the impacts of fuel economy improvement between MY 1976 and MY 1979 are properly attributable to the AFES program. From this viewpoint, the manufacturers plans are not really voluntary once a standard requires them to comply with their plans. In addition, this view recognizes that the voluntary plans were prompted, at least in part, by the knowledge that an average fuel economy standard would be in effect in MY 1979. On the other hand, it can be argued that the only impact brought about by the AFES results from manufacturers' actions to meet the AFES over and above their voluntary plans. From this viewpoint, all other impacts would happen regardless of whether the AFES were established, and are, therefore, not attributable to it.
Both of the viewpoints just discussed have merit.

Therefore, rather than rejecting one in favor of the other, the agency decided to analyze the environmental impact from both points of view.
By way of introduction, the agency analysis of fuel economy improvement potential for MY 1979 indicates that such improvements will come about through reducing the average weight of the vehicles (through materials substitutions, redesigning certain components, or taking iron and

steel out of the vehicle), reduction in vehicle performance by reducing cubic inch displacement (CID) of the engines (i.e., using smaller engines) or modifying the total drive ratio (N/V), and improvements in engine and drivetrain technology, including modifications in emissions control systems. The agency believes that most environmental impacts of the standard, other than the decrease in fuel consumption, will result from manufacturers employing one, some, or all of these fuel economy improvement techniques.
1 ...
The agency chose MY 1976 as the base period from which to develop the AFES and to evaluate its environmental impact. The baseline for all projections is the EPA 1976 Light Duty Truck Data Base. For fuel economy projections, the 49 State (Federal) MY 1976 fuel economy for catalyst equipped vehicles was used. 1976 was chosen as the base year because it is the latest model year for which accurate hard data on vehicle attributes, fuel economy, and production mix exist. Moreover, MY 1976 reflects the most recent consumer buying habits in terms of production mix. It is assumed for GM and Ford that their captive imports are a part of their production. However, little fuel economy improvement is projected for captive imports between MY 1976 and MY 1979, and their effect on fleet average fuel economy is considered based on their 1976 sales volumes.

Total domestic production in MY 1979 was assumed to be 1 million vehicles of which 52.6 percent were GM, 27.9 percent were Ford, 16.3 percent were Chrysler, and 3.7 percent were AMC. Additionally, it was assumed that GM and Ford would each sell 50,000 captive imports in MY 1979.
* .
A. Water Quality and Water Supply: Water quality and industrial water supply demand will be impacted by changes in the use of steel, cast iron, aluminum, and plastics in the manufacture of NPA's. The agency expects that the use of steel and cast iron could decrease as a result of weight reduction and CID reduction.
The agency expects that the use of aluminum and plastics could increase as these materials are substituted for iron and steel for purposes of reducing total vehicle weight.
From the viewpoint that all impacts of improving fuel economy from MY 1976 levels to a level where all manufacturers can meet the proposed AFES are attributable to the AFES, the total savings in cast iron and steel would be approximately 42 million pounds. From the viewpoint that only those impacts resulting from actions by GM and Chrysler to meet the AFES over and above their voluntary plans for MY 1979 are attributable to the standard, the total savings in cast iron and steel would be 24.8

million pounds. The total additional use of aluminum and plastics would be 5.26 million pounds each. Since no manufacturer indicated a plan to use material substitutions as a fuel economy improvement measure, the additional use of aluminum or plastics is applicable to both viewpoints. The analyses by which the agency estimates the magnitude of the change in material use is discussed more fully in Section I. Natural Resources.
For either viewpoint, the decrease in the production of steel and cast iron is likely to result in a small improvement in the Nation's water quality and a small decrease in industrial water supply demand. The relationship of these improvements are assumed to be proportional to the percentage decrease in total steel consumption and the amount of pollutants discharged. For a total national consumption of 236.2 billion pounds in 1975, the reductions insteel and cast iron consumptions from both viewpoints would be 0.018 percent and 0.010 percent respectively. Likewise the increased consumption of aluminum and plastics is likely to result in a small decrease in the Nation's water quality and an increase in industrial water supply demand. For either viewpoint, the increase in the use of aluminum is 0.055 percent of

total national consumption in 1975 of 9.6 billion pounds, and the increase in the use of plastics is 0.025 percent of total national consumption in 1975 of 21.2 billion pounds.
B. <u>Solid Waste</u>: The agency believes that the additional use of 5.26 million pounds of plastics is likely to result in a minor increase in the solid waste disposal problem, particularly with respect to recycling.
At the present time, little of the additional plastics would be recycled. However, this may change as basic resources become less available and therefore more valuable. The degree to which recycling becomes available as a disposal technique is dependent upon political and economic factors and the availability of sanitary landfills, pyrolytic furnaces, and solid waste handling and sorting machinery. The automobile is considered a likely candidate for resource recovery because of the relatively high value of the materials and the fact that they can be brought to the site of the recovery facility in a unit. However, the variety of materials present in automobiles hampers the efforts to increase resource recovery.
The Bureau of Mines of the U.S. Department of Interior has investigated the disposal problem as reported in their Information Circular 8596, Bureau of Mines Research Programs

on Recycling and Disposal of Mineral-, Metal-, and Energy-Based Wastes, dated 1973. This document discusses extensively the reclamation of materials from junked automobiles. With regard to the reuse of discarded plastics, the Bureau has found that polyethelene, polystyrene, polyvinyl chloride, and polypropylene, which are over 85 percent of discarded plastics, can be separated and then reformed. Separation of the waste thermoplastics has been achieved using a combination of techniques. Waste polyvinyl chloride can be broken down into a valuable chemical reagent and char suitable for use as a fuel.
For the present analysis, the agency assumes that none of the additional plastics will be recycled.

Incineration and deposit in sanitary landfills provide the normal method by which to dispose of nonrecyclable wastes. The Society of the Plastics Industries, Inc. reports that burning 2 to 4 percent plastics with other refuse in incinerators does not damage the incinerators or significantly change the composition of the effluent gas. However, the agency recognizes the preliminary nature of the SPI study and neither endorses nor refutes this finding.
When deposited in sanitary landfills, plastics and other light objects tend to rise over a period of time.

Plastics, in particular, do not readily decompose.

Thus, infusion of a substantial quantity of plastics

will tend to put off the time when the landfill can be

put to other uses. Moreover, deposit of almost any

materials will fill up a landfill sooner, requiring greater
\nuse of land for sanitary landfills.
C. <u>Noise Levels</u>: The Agency believes that mo appreciable incease in noise levels are likely to result from the AFES for MY 1979. The manufacturers do not plan large scale reductions in sound absorption materials or weight reduction means. Also, the manufacturers plan only very limited application of diesel engines in MY 1979.
There is a possibility that noise levels will increase slightly due to manufacturers' plans to substitute 6 cylinder and smaller V-8 engines for larger V-8 engines. Inquiries have been made to determine if data were available to answer the noise problem associated with this shift.
Research is underway at DOT and EPA to determine the relation of engine size to noise. Presently, there is little data of substantive value to provide a clear insight into the problem. Most data has been collected

under test conditions which identify maximum noise levels but do not relate to the community noise problems.

These tests were conducted under acceleration conditions involving wide open throttles. It was also assumed that even though the engine size is reduced the drivers will continue to accelerate at the same rate, all other conditions remaining the same. Testing in this manner will produce increases in noise levels because of increased engine RPM. However, these tests do not represent actual operating conditions which may effect the community. Plans are underway to develop noise standards for motor vanicles which will be more representative of their operation in communities. It is anticipated that reductions of engine size, resulting from this standard, will have an imperceptible effect on community noise levels.
D. Radiation: no impact.

E. <u>Pesticides</u>, <u>Herbicides</u>, <u>Rodenticides</u>, <u>and</u> <u>Fungicides</u>: no impact. 
F. Esthetic and Other Considerations: no impact.
G. Hazardous or Toxic Materials: no impact.
H. Gaseous Emissions: no impact.
I. Natural Resources.

If the impact of the AFES upon use of cast iron and steel is assessed from the view point that all fuel economy measures likely to be taken to improve fuel economy from MY 1976 levels to the level established by the AFES, are attributable to the AFES, then the impact of the AFES upon cast iron and steel is likely to be a reduction in consumption of cast iron and steel by 42 million pounds. This reduction is the result of reductions in average engine size (CID) and average vehicle weight. The magnitude of the reduction was calculated as follows:
• · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · ·
The Agency derived a relationship between percent reduction in CID, and percent reduction in vehicle weight. This was done by comparing the average weight and average CID of a vehicle fleet representative of the industry before the shift to smaller engines, with the average weight and average CID of the fleet after the shift to smaller engines. As a result of this comparison, the agency estimates that the percent weight reduction in cast iron and steel is equal to 0.109 multiplied by the percent CID reduction. If this relationship is applied to the amount of CID reduction which is likely to result to achieve compliance with the proposed AFES, the savings in cast iron and steel is approximately 18.2 million pounds.

. .
In addition to cast iron and steel saved through reduction in CID, the agency believes that a reduction in vehicle weight is likely to result from General Motors' efforts to reach the standard. This reduction in vehicle weight is estimated to result in a 45 pound per vehicle reduction in cast iron and steel, in a fleet of approximately 526,000 vehicles, for a total reduction of 23.7 million pounds due to reducing average vehicle weight.
• ,
If the impact of the AFES upon cast iron and steel usage is assessed from the viewpoint that the only impacts resulting from manufacturers taking steps to improve fuel economy over what they indicated in their product plans for MY 1979, the impact would be a savings of 24.8 million pounds. This amount of savings is derived from the savings due to CID reductions beyond manufacturers plans (approximately 1.1 million pounds, as derived from the relationship between CID reduction and weight reduction discussed above), and the 23.7 million pounds due to vehicle weight reduction.
The agency assumed that the production of cast iron and steel against which these savings should be measured was 236.2 billion pounds, the total national consumption for 1975. Thus, a savings of 42 million pounds is a savings of 0.018 percent of total national consumption

of cast iron and steel, and a savings of 24.8 million pounds represents a savings of 0.010 percent of national consumption.

The agency believes that the use of an additional 10 pounds of plastic and an additional 10 pounds of aluminum per vehicle as part of a weight reduction program for General Motors is likely to result from the AFES.

This results in a total increase in each of 5.26 million pounds which is 0.055 percent of the national consumption of aluminum and 0.025 percent of the national consumption of plastics.
The above impacts on natural resources were based on a scenario that assumed for a fleet of vehicles, a ten percent shift in vehicle inertia weight class (see the EPA regulation, Revised Light Duty Truck Regulations for 1979 and Later Model Year Vehicles - 40 FR 56316,

December 28, 1976 for definition of inertia weight) for a 50 pound reduction in vehicle weight for each vehicle. Since only 10 percent of the vehicles shift intertia weight class, the 50 pound weight reduction could be applied to only those vehicles which would shift classes. The tested fuel economy would be the same as if all vehicles lost the 50 pounds whereas the real world fuel economy

improvement would only reflect the loss of 50 pounds in 10 percent of the vehicles. If the means of reducing the weight of vehicles by 50 pounds is costly, it can be assumed that it would only be applied to 10 percent of the vehicles and the cost possibly spread over all vehicles. If the cost of the weight reduction is relatively small it can be presumed that the 50 pound weight reduction would be applied to all vehicles because of the resulting marketing benefits and the fact the future weight reductions could cause more inertia weight class shifts. The scenario developed for this standard included relatively low cost methods of reducing weight. If GM improves fuel economy by this means, it is presumed that all vehicles would lose the 50 pounds. Thus, the determination of national resources savings were based on the full application of 50-pound weight reduction to the GM fleet.
